newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico defends farmers in U.S. strawberry scare.
newsitem.headline: Mexico defends farmers in U.S. strawberry scare.

text.p: Mexico defended its strawberry farmers on Friday and said an outbreak of the hepatitis A virus in the United States was not clearly linked to exports of the fruit from Mexico.

At least 175 schoolchildren in Michigan, and possibly many more in other states, contracted the virus in recent weeks after eating frozen strawberries that were part of a government school lunch programme.
U.S. officials are trying to determine how the strawberries became tainted and whether they came from Mexico. Suppliers must vouch that only U.S. products are used in school lunches.
"It has not been confirmed that the origin of the fruit is Mexico," Mexico's Deputy Agriculture Minister Romarico Arroyo told Radio Red, a private radio station, on Friday.
Arroyo said tainted Mexican food products had entered the United States in previous years, but he doubted Mexican farmers were at fault in this case now that tougher import laws were in force.
He said if the strawberries were shipped nearly a year ago, as has been reported, then the fruit could easily have been contaminated during packaging in the United States.

He also said the volumes of strawberries involved indicated it was not a case of just one tainted shipment, but a problem in the processing. The fruit was packaged by Williamson Sales Co. of San Diego. The company is under investigation by U.S. officials.

"A plant that commits the offence of using an imported product in a programme in which it is banned, tantamount to contraband, could also be suspected of breaking standards, such as sanitary levels," Arroyo said.
Agriculture Ministry officials travelled to San Diego Friday to discuss the issue with U.S. officials. The meetings were still going on late on Friday.
Producers in Mexican strawberry farming states strongly rejected the notion that any contaminated strawberries came from their fields.

"Strawberry producers and processors in this region -- known internationally for its strawberry quality -- demand the situation be clarified and (Mexico) vindicated," Francisco Leon, the leader of strawberry growers from Guanajuato state told news agency Notimex.

About 26 million children receive hot meals daily at 90,000 schools under the federal school lunch programme, which costs the U.S. government several billion dollars a year. The programme, run by the Agriculture Department, subsidises the cost of meals to poor children and provides food donations.
